name: Path of Least Resistance
description: Choose a new angle or target when a BJJ attack meets a strong barrier. Learn what to keep, what to change, and when rebuilding control is better than switching moves.
summary: When a defense blocks one route, look for a better angle or target while keeping the control that makes a new attack possible.
overview: A stiff frame is information about the direction it resists. Sometimes you can move around it; sometimes you need to remove it, or stop attacking and restore your balance first.
key_takeaways: Identify the obstacle before changing technique: a post, frame, hook, grip, or body angle.
Change one useful thing at a time, such as your angle around a frame or the direction of an off-balance.
Keep the grips and connections that still serve the next action.
Do not confuse an easier-looking opening with a safer one; check what a switch exposes.
Redirect after a meaningful attempt, not at the first sign that the opponent will resist.

bjj_applications.scenario: An open guard player’s feet stop your forward passing pressure
bjj_applications.application: Keep your balance and work to redirect or clear a leg before approaching from the side. Driving harder into both extended legs repeats the same problem.
bjj_applications.outcome: The next attempt addresses the barrier instead of adding force in its strongest direction.

bjj_applications.scenario: Your butterfly sweep meets a firm post
bjj_applications.application: Notice which arm or leg is supporting them. Keep your upper-body connection while changing the angle or preparing an attack that deals with that post.
bjj_applications.outcome: The defense tells you what must change before another sweep attempt.

bjj_applications.scenario: A mount attack draws both hands to the neck
bjj_applications.application: Look for an exposed elbow while preserving your base. If the elbows remain tight, improve the existing choke grips or position instead of reaching for an arm that is still protected.
bjj_applications.outcome: You use an available opening without treating a neck defense as an automatic armbar.

common_mistakes.mistake: Changing attacks before establishing any control
common_mistakes.consequence: Every new move starts from a worse connection than the last.
common_mistakes.correction: Keep the current setup until you can name the barrier and a workable replacement.

common_mistakes.mistake: Backstepping over a trapped leg just to avoid a knee shield
common_mistakes.consequence: Your leg and balance may remain controlled as your torso turns away.
common_mistakes.correction: Free or account for the entanglement before changing your passing direction.

training_exercises.name: Find the barrier
training_exercises.description: Start with a familiar guard pass and let bottom provide one clear defense. Pause before forcing through it, identify the obstructing contact, then try an angle change. Reset when the pass settles or guard is recovered; increase resistance once the route is clear.
training_exercises.focus: Choose a change that addresses the actual obstruction.

training_exercises.name: Keep one connection
training_exercises.description: Start in butterfly guard with an agreed upper-body grip. Top defends the first sweep with a post; bottom explores a second direction while retaining useful contact. Reset on a sweep, pass, lost connection, or tap.
training_exercises.focus: Redirect without starting the whole exchange again.

knowledge_assessment.question: Should resistance always make you switch techniques?
knowledge_assessment.answer: No. First check whether the original attack lacks a grip, angle, or balance break that you can still obtain.
